Follow clusters across time windows

Source: R/merge_dynamic_clusters.R
merge_dynamic_clusters.Rd

When clusters are detected in each time window separately, their identifiers mean nothing from one window to the next: cluster "01" of the 1975-1984 network and cluster "01" of the 1976-1985 network may be two different literatures. merge_dynamic_clusters() links the clusters of successive windows that share most of their nodes, and gives them a common identifier, so that a cluster becomes an entity that can be born, persist and disappear. This is the step that turns a series of networks into a history of research communities, in the spirit of the alluvial maps of Rosvall and Bergstrom (2010) .

The rule is a double majority. Let \(V_a\) be the nodes of cluster \(a\) in window \(t-1\) and \(V_b\) those of cluster \(b\) in window \(t\). Cluster \(b\) inherits the identifier of \(a\) when most nodes of \(a\) go to \(b\) and most nodes of \(b\) come from \(a\): $$\frac{|V_a \cap V_b|}{D_a} > \tau \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{|V_a \cap V_b|}{D_b} > \tau,$$ with \(\tau\) the threshold_similarity. The denominators depend on similarity_type: with "complete", \(D_a = |V_a|\) and \(D_b = |V_b|\); with "partial", only the nodes present in both windows count, \(D_a = |V_a \cap V_t|\) and \(D_b = |V_b \cap V_{t-1}|\), \(V_t\) being all the nodes of window \(t\). Since \(\tau > 0.5\), a cluster can inherit at most one identifier, and an identifier passes to at most one cluster. A cluster that meets no match gets a new identifier.

Usage

merge_dynamic_clusters(
  list_graph,
  cluster_id,
  node_id,
  threshold_similarity = 0.5001,
  similarity_type = c("complete", "partial")
)

Arguments

list_graph

A list of at least two tbl_graphs in chronological order (oldest first), as produced by build_dynamic_networks() and add_clusters().

cluster_id

Character scalar, the node column with the clusters of each window (e.g. "cluster_leiden").

node_id

Character scalar, the node column with an identifier that is stable across windows (e.g. "source_id").

threshold_similarity

Number in \((0.5, 1]\), the threshold \(\tau\). Higher values require more similar clusters and create more distinct dynamic clusters.

similarity_type

"complete" or "partial", see the description. Required: there is no default, as the choice changes the results.

Value

The list of graphs, with the same names, where nodes have a new column dynamic_{cluster_id} (e.g. dynamic_cluster_leiden, with identifiers "cl_1", "cl_2"...) and edges the columns dynamic_{cluster_id}_from, dynamic_{cluster_id}_to and dynamic_{cluster_id} (missing for edges between clusters).

Details

Which windows? The rule needs nodes present in successive windows. In a network of documents (e.g. bibliographic coupling), each document has a single date, so successive windows (overlapping_window = FALSE in build_dynamic_networks()) share no node and no cluster can be matched: use sliding windows. Successive windows work when nodes persist over time, as cited references (co-citation), authors or journals do; two windows may still share no node when the literature changed completely.

Complete or partial? With sliding windows, the network of window \(t\) loses the documents of the first year of window \(t-1\) and gains those of a new year; in a growing literature, newcomers can be numerous. With "complete", a cluster that keeps all its past members but doubles with newcomers cannot inherit the identifier, because its members coming from \(a\) are less than half of it: the cluster is considered new because its composition changed. With "partial", the newcomers are ignored and the same cluster keeps its identifier. Which one is right depends on what a cluster is taken to be: a group of documents (complete), or a structure that recruits new documents (partial).

What the rule does not do. Clusters are compared only with the previous window: a cluster that vanishes for one window and comes back gets a new identifier. Splits and merges are not recorded as such: the part that meets the double majority keeps the identifier, the others are new. With \(\tau\) close to 0.5, small fluctuations of the partition (a stochastic algorithm, a resolution change) may break or create continuities; it is good practice to compare the results for a few thresholds and seeds.

References

Rosvall M, Bergstrom CT (2010). “Mapping Change in Large Networks.” PLoS ONE, 5(1), e8694. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0008694 .

See also

name_clusters() with name_merged_clusters = TRUE to label the dynamic clusters; networks_to_alluv() and plot_alluvial() to draw their evolution.

Examples

networks <- build_dynamic_networks(
  nodes = subset(Nodes_stagflation, source_type == "Stagflation"),
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  time_variable = "source_year",
  time_window = 10,
  cooccurrence_method = "coupling_similarity",
  edges_threshold = 1,
  verbose = FALSE
)
#> Warning: The last window is shorter than the others.
#> ℹ The data end in 2013, but the last window ends in 2014.
networks <- add_clusters(
  networks,
  clustering_method = "leiden",
  objective_function = "modularity",
  seed = 123,
  verbose = FALSE
)

networks <- merge_dynamic_clusters(
  networks,
  cluster_id = "cluster_leiden",
  node_id = "source_id",
  threshold_similarity = 0.51,
  similarity_type = "partial"
)
#> Warning: 3 pairs of consecutive windows share no node: their clusters cannot be matched.
#> ℹ Clusters are matched through the nodes they share. In a network of documents
#>   (coupling), each node has one date: use sliding windows (`overlapping_window
#>   = TRUE` in `build_dynamic_networks()`). If windows already slide, the nodes
#>   may have changed completely, or the threshold may leave a window without
#>   edges.
networks[[2]]
